title: HUAWEI’s first continuous glucose monitor is here, costs just under $50
summary: Expect a MARD value of 7.06%, up to 16 days of use, and (unfortunately) a China-only release.
body: Credit: HUAWEI TL;DR HUAWEI has launched the Sense G1 continuous glucose monitor in China. The device lets users view their glucose levels via a connected phone or wearable and offers updates every minute. The Sense G1 costs ~$45 in its home market, but we hope it eventually releases outside China. HUAWEI confirmed earlier this month that it would launch its first continuous glucose monitor (CGM) , dubbed the Sense G1. We didn’t get pricing and availability details back then, but the firm has now launched the device in China. The Sense G1 CGM is the firm’s first Class III medical device and allows users to view their glucose levels via a connected phone or wearable. In fact, you can view your levels on a HUAWEI watch by simply raising your wrist. HUAWEI explains that the CGM offers updates every minute and has a warm-up time of 30 minutes. You can also get alerts for abnormal blood sugar levels, such as high/low levels and emergency low blood sugar. As for measurement accuracy, the manufacturer promises a Mean Absolute Releative Difference (MARD) value of 7.06%.

title: Samsung’s Tizen-based Galaxy Watch gets an unofficial Wear OS 3.5 port
summary: Eight years later, there's potentially more life in this old watch.
body: TL;DR A developer has released an unofficial Wear OS 3.5 port based on Android 11 for the original Samsung Galaxy Watch (SM-R800). The port uses Pixel Watch software and reportedly supports Gemini, the Play Store, GPS, and health tracking. The port and installation guide are available on GitHub, though it remains experimental. Samsung’s switch from Tizen to Wear OS in 2021 opened up a whole new world of apps and Google services for Galaxy Watch owners. But you needed a Galaxy Watch 4 or newer to enjoy those benefits. Older models were left behind, and as Samsung wound down its Tizen smartwatch ecosystem , their usefulness gradually diminished. However, one developer is giving the original Galaxy Watch another shot at life. A developer known as Depth118 has shared an unofficial Android 11-based Wear OS 3.5 port on GitHub for Samsung’s 2018 Galaxy Watch. The project uses software from the original Google Pixel Watch, which, despite launching four years later, shares the same Exynos 9110 processor. The port is specifically designed for the 46mm Bluetooth Galaxy Watch (SM-R800), and the list of features the developer claims to have working is surprisingly extensive.

title: The best Android keyboard app isn’t on the Play Store. Here’s how to install it
summary: HeliBoard brings customization, clipboard history and offline typing to Android, without Google’s data collection.
body: Credit: Dhruv Bhutani / Android Authority Android’s always been the go-to destination when it comes to customisation and dialing in the experience exactly as you want it, and that extends to switching out the keyboard for something a bit more bespoke. For the longest time, finding a good keyboard for Android usually meant choosing between Gboard and SwiftKey . Both are excellent at predicting what you’re going to type, correcting spelling mistakes and letting you swipe between letters. The catch is that both these keyboards are made by mega corps, Google and Microsoft, and data collection is part and parcel of the deal. That’s why I’ve been looking at HeliBoard. It’s a free, open-source keyboard that offers many of the same features you’d expect from a modern Android keyboard without needing an internet connection, and, most importantly, no data collection. There are no advertisements, no cloud-based processing and plenty of customization options as is to be expected with open-source apps. There’s just one catch, you won’t find the app on the Google Play Store.

title: Google gives publishers more visibility in AI Mode with new ‘Dive Deeper’ links
summary: Google wants curiosity to extend beyond AI-generated answers.
body: TL;DR Google has started rolling out its previously announced “Dive Deeper” section in Search’s AI Mode. The section displays prominent blue links, image thumbnails, and descriptions of related articles below AI-generated responses. The change aims to encourage further exploration of topics while giving publishers more visibility in AI-powered search results. Google’s efforts to turn Search into an answer engine have left publishers fighting for clicks and some users missing the depth that traditional search results offered. While AI Mode has made researching topics less time-consuming, Google recognizes that getting a quick answer isn’t always the end of someone’s search journey. To address this, the company is now rolling out a new “Dive Deeper” section in AI Mode to encourage readers to explore articles beyond its AI-generated answers. SEO consultant Glenn Gabe spotted and shared the change on X (via Search Engine Roundtable ). The section appears at the bottom of AI Mode responses and features prominent blue links, image thumbnails, and descriptions explaining what each article offers. It’s one of several improvements Google announced last month.
